summary: Four friends lower a paralyzed man through a roof, and Jesus forgives his sins, then heals him to prove He has the right to forgive.
key_insight: The friends came for a healing, and Jesus spoke first about sins. The scribes were right that only God can forgive sins. That is the very point Jesus went on to prove.
story: Jesus came back to Capernaum, His own city, {Mt} and word spread that He was in the house. So many people gathered that there was no room left, not even near the door, and He preached the word to them. {Mk} Pharisees and teachers of the law were sitting nearby, men who had come from every town of Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem, and the power of the Lord was present to heal. {Lk}

Then four men arrived, carrying a paralyzed friend on a bed. {Mk} They could not get him through the crowd, so they went up on the housetop, {Lk} opened up the roof above Jesus, {Mk} and let the man down with his bed through the tiling, into the middle of the room, right in front of Jesus. {Lk}
When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralyzed man, “Son, be of good cheer; your sins are forgiven you.” {Mt}

Some of the scribes began reasoning in their hearts, “Why does this Man speak blasphemies like this? Who can forgive sins but God alone?” {Mk} Jesus knew their thoughts at once and said, “Why do you reason about these things in your hearts? Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven you,’ or to say, ‘Arise, take up your bed and walk’?” {Mk}
“But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins,” He said, and then He turned to the paralyzed man: “I say to you, arise, take up your bed, and go to your house.”

Immediately the man rose up in front of them all, picked up the bed he had been lying on, and went home glorifying God. {Lk} Everyone was amazed. They glorified God and were filled with fear, saying, “We have seen strange things today!” {Lk}
differences: Only Mark mentions the four men and the digging through the roof; Luke says they let him down “through the tiling.” Matthew does not mention the roof at all.
Jesus calls the man “Son” in Matthew and Mark, and “Man” in Luke. Matthew adds “be of good cheer.”
Luke alone says the religious leaders had come from all over Galilee, Judea and Jerusalem, and that “the power of the Lord was present to heal.”
The crowd’s response differs in wording: “We never saw anything like this!” (Mark), “We have seen strange things today!” (Luke), and glory to God “who had given such power to men” (Matthew).

fit.question: Mark says the men dug through the roof. Luke says they let the man down through the tiles. Which was it?

points.label: Luke’s word for his readers
points.text: Luke wrote for Greek readers who knew tiled roofs. He describes the scene in terms they could picture, as a good storyteller does.

points.label: Both can be true
points.text: Many roofs in Galilee were wooden beams covered with branches and packed clay, and some had tiles laid over part of them. Lifting tiles and breaking through the packing describe the same act from two angles.

fit.note: Two witnesses describe one hole in one roof in their own words. Nothing here requires an error.
fit.short: Mark describes breaking through the roof; Luke speaks of tiles, a picture his Greek readers knew. Both describe opening the roof.

scene.label: The house
scene.text: Mark says Jesus was “in the house” in Capernaum. This was probably the home where He was staying, possibly Peter’s house, where He had healed Peter’s mother-in-law (Mark 1:29).

scene.label: Flat roofs
scene.text: Roofs were flat, reached by an outside stair, and made of beams laid with branches and packed clay. Opening one was messy work, but it could be repaired.

scene.label: Only God forgives
scene.text: The scribes knew the Scriptures well: sin is against God, so only God can forgive it (Isaiah 43:25). That is why Jesus’ words sounded to them like blasphemy.

scene.label: “Son of Man”
scene.text: This was Jesus’ favorite name for Himself. It comes from Daniel 7:13–14, where one like a Son of Man receives authority and a kingdom from God.

witnesses.matthew: Tells the story briefly and places it in a chain of miracles (chapters 8–9) that show the King’s authority over sickness, storms, demons and now sin. He ends with the crowds glorifying God “who had given such power to men.”
witnesses.mark: Gives the vivid details: the crowd blocking the door, the four friends, the broken roof. This is the first of five conflict stories in Mark (2:1–3:6) that end with leaders plotting to destroy Jesus.
witnesses.luke: Notes that teachers of the law had come from everywhere to watch Jesus, and that the Lord’s power was present to heal. Luke, who loves to record praise, shows both the healed man and the crowd glorifying God.

seeing.reveals: Jesus claims to do what only God can do, forgive sins, and then proves it with a healing everyone can see. The visible miracle confirms the invisible pardon.
seeing.living: Jesus saw “their faith,” the faith of friends who would not stop at a crowded door. Bring people to Jesus even when it costs you effort and dignity. And remember that your deepest need, and theirs, is forgiveness, which He gives first.
seeing.ponder: Who do you need to carry to Jesus, and what “roof” stands between them and Him?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus forgives what only God can forgive, and He proves it.
outline: Faith that will not be stopped (1–4)
A word only God can speak (5–7)
preaching.watch_for: This is the first of five conflict stories in Mark 2:1–3:6. The tension grows from silent questions in the heart (2:6) to an open plot to destroy Jesus (3:6).

title: A Paralyzed Man Through the Roof
